Threat.value: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room

vignette:
Mai is a 51-year-old dentist who runs a small practice in a suburban strip mall. Three years ago, a former patient—a man she had treated only twice—began leaving notes on her car windshield, then started appearing in the waiting room without appointments, and eventually waited across the street from her home in a parked sedan. She recognized him from the dental records, and when she called the police, they took a report but told her there was little they could do unless he made a direct threat. The notes grew more personal, referencing the songs she played in her office during his appointments. One note included a lyric from a ballade she used to hum while working; after that, every time she heard that melody—on the radio, in a store, even in her own head—she felt the same cold twist in her stomach, as though he were still standing behind her. She stopped listening to music altogether when she drove or worked, and told her staff to keep the office sound system off, claiming it distracted her.

The stalking lasted seven months. She never knew when he would appear. Once, she spotted his car in the parking lot of a grocery store and fled through the back exit, leaving her cart full. Another time, she saw a local news segment about a similar case and had to leave the room, her heart hammering so hard she thought she might pass out. After that, she avoided all true-crime media, flipping channels past any suspenseful trailer, and she unsubscribed from several podcasts she had once enjoyed. Her husband tried to reassure her that the man had eventually moved away—the police confirmed he had left the state—but Mai could not let herself trust that. She had come to believe that safety was something that could vanish without warning, no matter what anyone told her. Even when her husband pointed out the locked doors and the alarm system, she found herself scanning the room for exits and positioning her chair so her back was against a wall.

At work, she rearranged the consultation office so her desk faced the door and the wall behind her was solid. She started refusing to sit in certain examination rooms where the layout left her exposed near a window. During lunch breaks, she would take her food into the storage area rather than sit in the staff lounge, because there she could lean against a metal shelf and watch the only entrance. Her hygienist noticed and asked if something was wrong; Mai said she was getting headaches from the fluorescent lights. The habit spread to every environment. When she and her husband went out to dinner, she would insist on a table in the corner, and if none was available, she would ask to leave before ordering. He grew frustrated, telling her that the restaurant was perfectly safe, but she felt a hot spike of fear each time someone walked up behind her. She began declining invitations to parties and social gatherings altogether, preferring the controlled space of her own home, where she knew every sightline and every lock.

Her marriage has become strained. Her husband wants to go on vacation, but Mai cannot imagine sitting on a beach with her back to the ocean, unable to see who might approach. When a police cruiser pulls up next to her at a red light, she shrinks in her seat, remembering the detective’s apologetic shrug—“Unless he does something concrete, ma’am…”—and she feels that same helplessness. She came to therapy after a panic attack in the dental office one afternoon. A patient’s phone played the opening bars of a pop song she had never heard before, but the first few notes were identical to the melody from the notes, and she froze mid-procedure, suddenly certain that she was about to see his face in the reflection of the instrument tray. She excused herself, locked the bathroom door, and cried. That night, she told her husband she could not keep living like this—always bracing, always positioning herself, always waiting for the threat to return. She is afraid, she said, that she will never feel at ease again, and she is equally afraid that if she lets her guard down, she will be proven right.
